# AGENTS.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Development Commands

Use Nub exclusively for dependency management, scripts, and TypeScript execution. The root `package.json` declares the workspaces and pins Nub; `.nvmrc` selects Node. Nub reads and writes the existing `pnpm-lock.yaml` without requiring pnpm.

Run scripts with `nub run`, repository TypeScript with `nub <file>`, and installed tools with `nub exec --node <tool>`. Keep third-party tools and built-package compatibility probes on plain Node; Nub's augmentation must not mask resolution errors or change test behavior. Use `nub install --frozen-lockfile` for reproducible installs and `nub add` / `nub remove` to manage dependencies.

Key commands:

- `nub run build` - Build all packages (runs recursive build command)
- `nub exec --node vitest run` - Run all tests with Vitest. Includes the compile-mode project, which re-runs the zod tests with global AOT compilation enabled (see `wiki/compile.md`).
- `nub exec --node vitest run <path>` - Run specific test file (e.g., `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/tests/string.test.ts`)
- `nub exec --node vitest run <path> -t "<pattern>"` - Run specific test(s) within a file (e.g., `-t "MAC"`)
- `nub exec --node vitest run --update` - Update all test snapshots
- `nub exec --node vitest run <path> --update` - Update snapshots for specific test file
- `nub run test:watch` - Run tests in watch mode
- `nub exec --node vitest run --coverage` - Run tests with coverage report
- `nub run test:compile` - Focused alias for just the compile-mode project. Already covered by `nub run test`; use this when iterating on compile-related changes.
- `nub run dev` - Execute TypeScript with Nub under source conditions
- `nub run dev <file>` - Execute `<file>` with Nub & proper resolution conditions. Usually use for `play.ts`.
- `nub run dev:play` - Quick alias to run play.ts for experimentation
- `nub run check:comments` - Fail on stacked `//` comment lines (`--fix` joins them)
- `nub run lint` - Run biome linter with auto-fix
- `nub run format` - Format code with biome
- `nub run fix` - Run both format and lint

## Rules

- Nub v0.8.3 and Node.js v24+ required; Nub provisions Node from `.nvmrc`
- ES modules are used throughout (`"type": "module"`)
- All tests must be written in TypeScript - never use JavaScript
- Use `play.ts` for quick experimentation; use proper tests for all permanent test cases
- Features without tests are incomplete - every new feature or bug fix needs test coverage
- Don't skip tests due to type issues - fix the types instead
- Test both success and failure cases with edge cases
- Keep added tests as minimal and dense as possible without sacrificing comprehensiveness; avoid redundant assertions or broad fixtures when a focused case proves the behavior.
- No log statements (`console.log`, `debugger`) in tests or production code
- Never stack prose across consecutive `//` lines. Lines have no maximum width here — the editor wraps for display — so a paragraph split across several `//` lines is just a hard-wrapped line, and hard wrapping breaks search, diffs and editing. Write one long `//` instead. `nub run check:comments` enforces this in pre-commit and CI; `--fix` joins the offenders. Commented-out code, `@ts-`/`@__NO_SIDE_EFFECTS__`-style pragmas, bullet lists, and blocks separated by a bare `//` are exempt. When two adjacent comments describe two different statements, separate them with a blank line rather than joining them.
- Keep comments SHORT AND TIGHT — one lowercase sentence fragment, one clause, no trailing period. Never a capitalized full sentence, and never two of them. Extreme concision: say only what the code cannot say, and cut the setup sentence, the recap, and the same point restated in different words; a comment that needs three sentences usually means the code should be clearer. Identifiers keep their real casing (`Error`, `parse()`), only the prose is lowercase.
- Ask before generating new files
- Use `util.defineLazy()` for computed properties to avoid circular dependencies
- Never branch on specific schema types in shared code. No `def.type === "optional"` conditionals, no hardcoded lists of wrapper type names, no walks up the wrapper chain hunting for a particular type. Every schema type added later silently falls through such a check, and the list is wrong the moment someone writes a new wrapper. When a shared path needs to know something about a schema, express it as a structural property on the internals — `optin`/`optout`, `values`, `pattern`, `propValues` — and let each type declare its own answer. This is not negotiable in the parse paths; a PR that adds edge-case conditional logic keyed on schema types will be rejected regardless of how well it is tested.
- Performance is critical - parameter reassignment is allowed for optimization
- Any change to `packages/zod/src` must be weighed on **all three axes: runtime performance, memory consumption, and bundle size** — see "The three axes" below. A change that improves one and is only checked on that one is not finished.
- ALWAYS use the `gh` CLI to fetch GitHub information (issues, PRs, etc.) instead of relying on web search or assumptions
- Keep JSDoc as minimal as possible. A self-explanatory type or symbol name needs no doc comment. When a comment is genuinely required, write one short sentence describing behavior — not history, rationale, or examples. Don't add interface-level JSDoc that just restates the interface name.
- When you've modified a PR (or opened/closed/commented on one), include the PR URL liberally in summary messages — at minimum once at the end of any reply that touched it
- When creating a PR, do not include a separate test plan section in the body. Link to any relevant issues under discussion, and use the same copywriting guidelines from "Commenting on issues and PRs": concise maintainer voice, prose over templates, and validation details only when they are material to the reader.
- Format validators (`z.iso.*`, `z.email()`, `z.url()`, `z.uuid()`, …) are deliberately narrower than the specs they're named after. "The spec allows X" is not a reason to accept X — see "Format validators: spec compliance is not the bar" below.
- NEVER bump the version in `packages/zod/package.json` (or any package's `package.json`), and NEVER run `gh workflow run release.yml`. Publishing is a maintainer-only dispatch behind an approval. If a version bump is genuinely needed, ask first.

## The three axes

Zod is judged on **runtime performance**, **memory consumption**, and **bundle size** at once, and they trade against each other constantly. Optimizing one in isolation is how regressions land: a change that buys bundle bytes can cost construction speed, and one that saves memory can cost both. Any non-trivial change to `packages/zod/src` — and any change to `core/` at all, since every build ships it — needs a number on all three before it is done. Report them together, including the ones that got worse.

`zod/mini` deserves its own line on the bundle axis: it is sold on size, so a fixed cost lands very differently there (~200 B is 6% of the smallest mini bundle and 1% of classic's).

| axis    | how to measure                                                                                                                                    |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| runtime | `packages/bench/*.ts` via `nub run bench <name>`, plus construction cost — parse and construction move independently                                 |
| memory  | `packages/bench/memory/schema-footprint.ts` and `realworld.ts` (retained bytes per schema; run under `--expose-gc`)                               |
| bundle  | bundle a `packages/treeshake` fixture with esbuild `--minify` under `--conditions=@zod/source` and gzip it, for both a classic and a mini fixture |

### Benchmarking traps

These produced hours of wrong conclusions; check them before believing a numbe

# Contributing

When it comes to open source, there are different ways you can contribute, all
of which are valuable. Here's a few guidelines that should help you as you prepare
your contribution.

## Initial steps

Before you start working on a contribution, create an issue describing what you want to build. It's possible someone else is already working on something similar, or perhaps there is a reason that feature isn't implemented. The maintainers will point you in the right direction.

<!-- ## Submitting a Pull Request

- Fork the repo
- Clone your forked repository: `git clone git@github.com:{your_username}/zod.git`
- Enter the zod directory: `cd zod`
- Create a new branch off the `master` branch: `git checkout -b your-feature-name`
- Implement your contributions (see the Development section for more information)
- Push your branch to the repo: `git push origin your-feature-name`
- Go to https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/compare and select the branch you just pushed in the "compare:" dropdown
- Submit the PR. The maintainers will follow up ASAP. -->

## Development

The following steps will get you set up to contribute changes to this repo:

Install [Nub](https://nubjs.com/docs) v0.8.3 first. Nub manages dependencies, runs scripts and TypeScript, and provisions the Node version in `.nvmrc`. The existing `pnpm-lock.yaml` is the lockfile format, not a requirement to install pnpm.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nubjs/nub/0ae8783f1f93763c56dfc827892cfb679e8a0a77/install.sh | bash -s -- 0.8.3
```

Restart the shell after installation so Nub is on `PATH`.

1. Fork this repo.

2. Clone your forked repo: `git clone git@github.com:{your_username}/zod.git`

3. Run `nub install --frozen-lockfile` to install dependencies.

4. Start playing with the code! You can do some simple experimentation in [`play.ts`](play.ts) (see `nub run dev:play` below) or start implementing a feature right away.

### Building Docs Locally

#### Dev Server

To start a dev server, run:

```sh
nub run --filter=@zod/docs dev
```

#### Production Build

To build `@zod/docs` for production, you will need to set the `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable to a personal access token. [Create a granular personal access token](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new) and accept the defaults (no extra permissions are necessary). Then:

```sh
export GITHUB_TOKEN=your_token_here # persists in shell session
nub run --filter=@zod/docs build
```

> The `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable is used to fetch stargazer counts of projects in Zod's ecosystem.

## Alternative: VSCode Dev Container setup

For an officially supported isolated dev environment that automatically installs dependencies for you:

1. `F1` in VSCode and start typing `Dev Containers: Clone Repository in Named Container Volume` to run the command.
2. For the repo, paste `git@github.com:{your_username}/zod.git` if you're using ssh.
3. Click `Create a new volume...` and name it `zod` and the folder name as `zod`.

Note: if you can't see `Dev Containers` in the `F1` menu, follow [this guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/devcontainers/tutorial) to install the needed extension.
In the OSS version of VSCode the extension may not be available.

### Commands

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `nub run build` | Build Zod and Zod Mini, including their declarations |
| `nub run test` | Run all Vitest projects, including compile mode and type checks |
| `nub run test:watch` | Start Vitest in watch mode |
| `nub run test <file>` | Run test files matching `<file>` |
| `nub run dev:play` | Execute [`play.ts`](play.ts) against source |
| `nub run dev:watch play.ts` | Re-run the playground when its imports change |
| `nub run --filter @zod/resolution test:all` | Check the built package's declarations and module resolution |
| `nub add -Dw <package>` | Add a root development dependency |

Run `nub run build` before testing built-package resolution and bundle sizes. Repository scripts use `nub exec --node` for third-party tools so tests retain plain Node semantics.

### Tests

Zod uses Vitest for testing. After implementing your contribution, write tests for it. Just create a new file in the `tests` directory of any workspace, or add additional tests to an existing file if appropriate.

> Zod uses git hooks to execute tests before `git push`. Before submitting your PR, run `nub run test` to make sure there are no (unintended) breaking changes.

### Documentation

The documentation site lives in `packages/docs` with content located at `packages/docs/content`. Be sure to document any API changes you implement.

Zod

TypeScript-first schema validation with static type inference
by @colinhacks


Docs   •   Discord   •   𝕏   •   Bluesky


### [Read the docs →](https://zod.dev/api)

## What is Zod? Zod is a TypeScript-first validation library. Define a schema and parse some data with it. You'll get back a strongly typed, validated result. ```ts import * as z from "zod"; const User = z.object({ name: z.string(), }); // some untrusted data... const input = { /* stuff */ }; // the parsed result is validated and type safe! const data = User.parse(input); // so you can use it with confidence :) console.log(data.name); ```
## Features - Zero external dependencies - Works in Node.js and all modern browsers - Tiny: `2kb` core bundle (gzipped) - Immutable API: methods return a new instance - Concise interface - Works with TypeScript and plain JS - Built-in JSON Schema conversion - Extensive ecosystem
## Installation ```sh npm install zod ```
## Basic usage Before you can do anything else, you need to define a schema. For the purposes of this guide, we'll use a simple object schema. ```ts import * as z from "zod"; const Player = z.object({ username: z.string(), xp: z.number(), }); ``` ### Parsing data Given any Zod schema, use `.parse` to validate an input. If it's valid, Zod returns a strongly-typed _deep clone_ of the input. ```ts Player.parse({ username: "billie", xp: 100 }); // => returns { username: "billie", xp: 100 } ``` **Note** — If your schema uses certain asynchronous APIs like `async` [refinements](https://zod.dev/api#refinements) or [transforms](https://zod.dev/api#transforms), you'll need to use the `.parseAsync()` method instead. ```ts const schema = z.string().refine(async (val) => val.length <= 8); await schema.parseAsync("hello"); // => "hello" ``` ### AOT compilation For hot validation paths, `z.compile(schema)` returns a schema clone with an ahead-of-time compiled fast path. Valid inputs take the compiled path; invalid inputs fall back to the regular parser so error reporting stays identical. Across a 55-schema benchmark the median speedup is **2.4x**, and it scales with how much work the schema does per parse: a large array of objects is ~9x, a 20-key object ~9x, a nested object ~4.5x, while a bare `z.string()` gains nothing — compilation removes per-node dispatch and allocation, and a single `typeof` has none to remove. ```ts const CompiledPlayer = z.compile(Player); CompiledPlayer.parse({ username: "billie", xp: 100 }); ``` To enable compilation globally for schemas constructed after import: ```ts import "zod/compile"; // place before modules that define schemas ``` Things to know: - Compilation uses `new Function`. Global mode is automatically disabled when `z.config({ jitless: true })` is set (e.g. CSP environments); calling `z.compile()` directly is an explicit opt-in. - Schemas with async refinements or transforms can't be compiled, and neither can a few other constructs. That is not an error: `z.compile()` hands the schema back unchanged and it keeps using the regular parser, exactly as global mode leaves it. Pass `{ strict: true }` to throw `ZodCompileAsyncError` / `ZodCompileUnsupportedError` instead. - On invalid input, refinements and transforms may run twice (fast path, then fallback). - Deriving a new schema from a compiled one (`.refine()`, `.extend()`, etc.) returns an uncompiled schema — compile the final schema. See [`compile` docs](https://zod.dev/compile) for details. ### Handling errors When validation fails, the `.parse()` method will throw a `ZodError` instance with granular information about the validation issues. ```ts try { Player.parse({ username: 42, xp: "100" }); } catch (err) { if (err instanceof z.ZodError) { err.issues; /* [ { expected: 'string', code: 'invalid_type', path: [ 'username' ], message: 'Invalid input: expected string, received number' }, { expected: 'number', code: 'invalid_type', path: [ 'xp' ], message: 'Invalid input: expected number, received string' } ] */ } } ``` To avoid a `try/catch` block, you can use the `.safeParse()` method to get back a plain result object containing either the successfully parsed data or a `ZodError`. The result type is a [discriminated union](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#discriminated-unions), so you can handle both cases conveniently. ```ts const result = Player.safeParse({ username: 42, xp: "100" }); if (!result.success) { result.error; // ZodError instance } else { result.data; // { username: string; xp: number } } ``` **Note** — If your schema uses certain asynchronous APIs like `async` [refinements](https://zod.dev/api#refinements) or [transforms](https://zod.dev/api#transforms), you'll need to use the `.safeParseAsync()` method instead. ```ts const schema = z.string().refine(async (val) => val.length <= 8); await schema.safeParseAsync("hello"); // => { success: true; data: "hello" } ``` ### Inferring types Zod infers a static type from your schema definitions. You can extract this type with the `z.infer<>` utility and use it however you like. ```ts const Player = z.object({ username: z.string(), xp: z.number(), }); // extract the inferred type type Player = z.infer; // use it in your code const player: Player = { username: "billie", xp: 100 }; ``` In some cases, the input & output types of a schema can diverge. For instance, the `.transform()` API can convert the input from one type to another. In these cases, you can extract the input and output types independently: ```ts const mySchema = z.string().transform((val) => val.length); type MySchemaIn = z.input; // => string type MySchemaOut = z.output; // equivalent to z.infer // number ```

report.overview: Zod is a dependency-free, TypeScript-first schema library that turns declarative runtime validators into statically inferred input and output types for Node.js, browsers, and plain JavaScript consumers. This repository contains the full fluent API, a smaller functional Zod Mini surface, a shared schema runtime, bidirectional codecs, JSON Schema conversion, a legacy v3 compatibility entrypoint, and an optional ahead-of-time compiler. It also includes the zod.dev Next.js documentation site, extensive compatibility and bundle-size test workspaces, benchmarks, and guarded npm/JSR release automation.

system_map.summary: The repository is a Nub-managed ESM monorepo whose principal deliverables are the `zod` and `@zod/mini` packages. Zod v4 is layered into a shared core, a fluent classic facade, and a functional mini facade; v3 remains published through a separate compatibility entrypoint. Runtime validation is entirely in-process, while the repository also contains a statically generated Next.js documentation application and maintenance scripts that access GitHub, npm, JSR, and the ISO currency source. Publishing is a manually dispatched, approval-gated GitHub Actions workflow rather than an automatic deployment from `main`.

claims.claim: The root workspace is private, ESM-only, pinned to Nub 0.8.3, and discovers packages through `packages/*`; root scripts build `zod` and `@zod/mini`, run Vitest, check formatting, linting, circular dependencies, version consistency, comments, and release lockstep.
The published `zod` package exposes root, mini, compile, locales, v3, v4, v4-mini, v4/mini, v4/core, and locale wildcard subpaths for source, ESM, CommonJS, and declarations.
The root `zod` entrypoint re-exports the v4 classic facade, while separate entrypoints route `zod/mini` to the v4 mini facade and `zod/v3` to the legacy implementation.

The v4 runtime boundary is explicit: `core/index.ts` exports constructors, parsers, schemas, checks, registries, compilation, and JSON Schema machinery; classic and mini compose those primitives into distinct public APIs.

Schema instances are trait-composed objects created through `$constructor`; their internal definitions, parse functions, traits, structural metadata, and deferred initialization live under a non-enumerable `_zod` property.

Runtime state is process-local rather than database-backed: global configuration and metadata registries are shared through `globalThis`, while parse-cycle state uses WeakMaps keyed by schemas, objects, and parse contexts.
The documentation application is a Next.js 15 and React 19 workspace using Fumadocs, Tailwind, Vercel Analytics, and Inkeep search/chat; its content is compiled from MDX collections.

Auxiliary workspaces separate concerns: `packages/bench` benchmarks competing validators, `packages/integration` type-checks Drizzle and AI SDK fixtures, `packages/resolution` verifies built module resolution, and `packages/treeshake` measures bundler behavior.
The normal build uses zshy to emit the packages and declarations, while package exports select raw TypeScript only under the private `@zod/source` condition used by repository development and tests.
Production documentation deployment is shaped for Vercel: the install command bootstraps the pinned Nub release, installs the monorepo lockfile, and then runs the repository build.

Release deployment is manual and approval-gated: the workflow tests, builds, validates package resolution, publishes both packages to npm and JSR with provenance, creates a GitHub release, and verifies the two packages remain version-aligned.

feature_catalog.summary: The primary user-facing product is a schema construction and validation API, offered in fluent classic and smaller functional mini forms. It supports primitive, structured, recursive, transforming, asynchronous, and bidirectional schemas, with both throwing and result-oriented execution APIs. AOT compilation and JSON Schema interoperability extend the runtime beyond ordinary interpretation. The repository's second user-facing surface is zod.dev, which exposes documentation, blog, search, generated social cards, RSS, and machine-readable LLM documentation endpoints.

claims.claim: Every classic schema exposes `parse`, `safeParse`, async variants, boolean `validate` methods, forward decode methods, backward encode methods, and safe async codec variants.

The schema catalog covers primitives and special values plus arrays, objects, records, tuples, unions, XOR unions, discriminated unions, intersections, maps, sets, enums, literals, files, promises, functions, lazy recursion, and custom schemas.

Built-in string validators include email, GUID and versioned UUIDs, URL and HTTP URL, emoji, NanoID, CUID/CUID2, ULID, XID, KSUID, IP and CIDR forms, MAC, Base64, E.164, credit card, IBAN, JWT, hostname, hex, currency codes, and hashes.
Object schemas support strip-by-default, strict, loose, and catchall modes, plus shape access, `keyof`, extension, picking, omission, partialization, requiredness, and deep-partial helpers.

Composable wrappers cover refinements, super-refinements, overwrites, optional/exact-optional/nonoptional, nullable/nullish, defaults, prefaults, catch values, arrays, unions, intersections, transforms, pipes, branding, readonly output, and metadata.
Codecs are bidirectional pipes with explicit decode and encode callbacks; `invertCodec` swaps their input/output schemas and forward/reverse transforms.
Function schemas can wrap implementations so arguments and return values are parsed synchronously or asynchronously at each call boundary.

`toJSONSchema` supports single schemas and registries, input/output views, draft 4, draft 7, draft 2020-12, OpenAPI 3.0, cycle and reuse policies, custom processors, overrides, external registries, and configurable handling of unrepresentable types.

`fromJSONSchema` converts boolean or object JSON Schemas back into Zod, recognizes composition, object, array, string, numeric, metadata, content, and OpenAPI keywords, and resolves local `$defs` or `definitions` references.
Schemas implement Standard Schema validation and Standard JSON Schema input/output conversion, allowing library-agnostic consumers to infer types, validate values, and request JSON Schema.
`z.compile(schema)` creates a compiled clone, `withParser` accepts an externally generated parser, and importing `zod/compile` enables lazy global compilation for subsequently constructed schemas.

Zod Mini reuses the same core schema implementations but exposes a smaller base instance API centered on functional factories and free parsing functions rather than the classic chain-heavy method surface.
The documentation site serves static catch-all docs pages, blog pages, local search, `/llms.txt`, `/llms-full.txt`, `/blog/rss.xml`, and dynamic Open Graph images.

data_flow.summary: A schema factory creates an immutable schema instance whose definition and structural capabilities are stored under `_zod`. Parsing sends a mutable payload and shared context through the schema graph; child schemas transform values and append raw issues, while the public boundary either returns a deep output structure or finalizes issues into a Zod error. Optional compilation replaces only the success path and deliberately delegates failure reporting to the interpreter. Separate conversion pipelines translate schema graphs to and from JSON Schema, while the documentation application turns MDX files into pages and text feeds.

claims.claim: Public factories delegate to core factory functions that instantiate a supplied schema class with a normalized definition, preserving one shared construction mechanism across classic and mini APIs.
`$ZodType` initializes checks, runs each check's attachment hooks, and selects either the raw parser or a parse-then-check runner; asynchronous checks are rejected from synchronous parse contexts.

A synchronous public parse creates `{value, issues: []}`, calls `schema._zod.run`, rejects unexpected promises, finalizes raw issues through configured error maps, and otherwise returns the transformed value.

Object parsing validates each declared string or symbol key through its child schema, builds a fresh result object, prefixes child issue paths, enforces optionality, and then strips, rejects, passes, or validates undeclared keys through the catchall policy.
Array, map, and set schemas allocate fresh output containers, run element schemas with the same parse context, prefix or nest element issues, and join child promises before returning.

The `optin` and `optout` structural metadata controls whether a parent may omit a slot, whether a default supplies a replacement, and whether undefined output should omit a property or shorten a tuple.

Safe parsing keeps failure construction lazy: callers can branch on `success` without immediately finalizing issues or constructing a ZodError, and reading or replacing `error` releases captured raw input state.

The cycle memoizer detects recursive schema graphs, allocates placeholder containers before descending, caches results per schema/input pair, resolves back-edges to those placeholders, and rejects cycles that pass through transforms.
Pipes run the input schema first and stop on substantive issues before invoking the output schema; codecs additionally transform between the sides and reverse direction when encoding.

Compilation walks the schema graph into generated source, hoists runtime constants and user callbacks into closure arguments, constructs a function with the `Function` constructor, and records whether an invalid sentinel is a definitive rejection.

A compiled schema sends valid inputs directly through its generated parser, but marks the context and invokes the original runtime parser on an invalid sentinel so canonical issue construction remains single-sourced.

JSON Schema emission traverses schemas into a shared `seen` map, invokes per-schema or registry processors, attaches metadata, extracts reused or cyclic nodes into definitions, applies overrides and deferred rewrites, and JSON-round-trips the final document.

JSON Schema ingestion first serializes and parses the input into a finite plain JSON graph, detects the target draft, indexes local definitions and references, converts the root, and registers recovered metadata.

Documentation content flows from generated Fumadocs MDX collections into route loaders; full LLM text rereads the underlying content files, removes frontmatter, runs the Remark pipeline, and concatenates pages in metadata order.

behavior_traces.summary: The most important flows begin at package import, schema construction, and a public parse call. The interpreted and compiled paths intentionally converge on the same runtime fallback for errors, while JSON Schema conversion follows a separate graph traversal. Recursive parsing adds a context-scoped memoization layer without changing the public parse contract. The documentation site has its own static content request path layered on top of Fumadocs and MDX.

claims.claim: Import trace: `src/index.ts` loads `v4/classic/external.ts`; that module exposes classic schemas, checks, errors, parse functions, core helpers, JSON Schema conversion, locales, ISO validators, and coercion factories.

Construction trace: `z.object(shape)` creates `ZodObject`; `ZodObject` ensures the default memoizer, initializes `$ZodObject`, initializes `ZodType`, attaches JSON Schema processing, and ultimately lets `$constructor` run deferred initializers and any global post-processor.

Successful sync parse trace: `schema.parse(data)` calls classic `parse.parse`, which calls core `_parse`, then `schema._zod.run`; an object run allocates a result, runs each child, merges property results, and returns the transformed value when no issues remain.

Failed sync parse trace: a leaf or container appends raw issues, parents prefix nested paths, `_parse` maps each issue through `finalizeIssue`, constructs the configured error class, restores a useful stack, and throws.
Safe parse trace: `_safeParse` runs the same schema graph but returns `{success: true, data}` or a failure object whose `error` getter creates and caches the finalized error only when accessed.

Async trace: `parseAsync` sets `ctx.async`, awaits promise-returning schema runs, then performs the same issue finalization; synchronous entrypoints instead throw `$ZodAsyncError` when a promise escapes.

Global compile trace: importing `zod/compile` installs `globalConfig.postProcessor`; each later schema receives a one-shot shim; its first eligible parse calls `compile(..., {strict:true})`, replaces itself with the compiled run on success, or permanently restores the interpreter on refusal.

Compiled failure trace: the generated parser returns `INVALID`; `withParser` sets the fallback flag and invokes the captured original run, preventing nested compiled wrappers from repeatedly executing user callbacks while preserving runtime-generated errors.

Cycle trace: a recursive container's memoized wrapper creates context state, caches an output placeholder before children parse, returns that placeholder on a repeated input visit, and records final issues after synchronous or asynchronous completion.

JSON Schema trace: `toJSONSchema` initializes the processor registry, calls `processSchema`, extracts definitions for cycles or reuse, finalizes references and metadata, and returns either one schema document or a registry map with shared definitions.

Docs request trace: the catch-all route resolves a page through `source.getPage`, derives LLM-friendly markdown with `getLLMText`, renders the compiled MDX body with shared components, and statically enumerates all routes through `source.generateParams`.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is broad and strongly integrated into normal development and CI. Vitest combines runtime assertions and TypeScript type checking, while a second project reruns the entire Zod test corpus with global AOT compilation enabled. Dedicated suites cover runtime semantics, compiler parity, JSON Schema conversion, cyclic data, package resolution, integrations, tree-shaking, and documentation consistency. Performance and randomized compiler fuzzing also exist, although the fuzzer is intentionally not part of deterministic CI.

claims.claim: The root Vitest configuration discovers every package project plus a dedicated compile-mode project, isolates tests, type-checks `*.test.ts`, and fails tests that write to console.
Compile mode includes every `packages/zod/src/**/*.test.ts` file, disables redundant type checking, and imports the production `zod/compile` side-effect module before tests.

The v4 classic suite is organized by schema behavior and includes focused files for objects, strings, codecs, cyclic data, optionality, registries, Standard Schema, JSON Schema, transforms, errors, and ReDoS cases.

The compiler has direct unit tests plus differential tests that compare success, issues, prototype identity, own-key order, symbols, array holes, frozen state, NaN, negative zero, thrown-error classes, and union branch soundness.
JSON Schema conversion has large dedicated suites in both directions, while core processors are also exercised by compile mode because they live under the same package project.
Bundle tests build real fixtures with esbuild, enforce gzip ceilings for classic and mini bundles, and assert that unrelated feature identifiers and regexes are absent after tree-shaking.

Built-package compatibility is tested separately: resolution tests run Are The Types Wrong and executable CJS/ESM probes, while integration fixtures type-check source and built packages under bundler, NodeNext, and Node16 CommonJS modes.

CI tests TypeScript 5.5, 6, and latest on Node LTS, builds before tests, runs integration and resolution checks, and separately enforces formatting, linting, comment style, and circular-dependency checks.
The release workflow repeats build, test, resolution, integration, lint, and circular-dependency checks before gaining publish permissions.

The seeded compiler fuzzer generates nested schema grammars and compares interpreted and compiled outputs, issues, and union behavior, but its header explicitly states that it is a hunting tool rather than a CI job.

Documentation-specific automated coverage is narrow: the checked-in docs test validates parity of code-block heights between classic and mini API tabs, while route rendering and external search/chat behavior have no corresponding route-level test file.

risk_map.summary: The core library has no authentication, database, or arbitrary filesystem surface, but it processes untrusted values and generates executable validation functions, so correctness and denial-of-service behavior are security-relevant. The code contains explicit mitigations for prototype pollution, cycles, ReDoS-prone formats, CSP restrictions, and duplicated callback execution. The documentation and automation layers introduce the repository's network, filesystem, token, and privileged CI boundaries. The largest maintenance risk is semantic drift among interpreted parsing, object JIT, AOT compilation, JSON Schema generation, classic, and mini surfaces.

claims.claim: AOT compilation uses the `Function` constructor and is incompatible with strict no-eval CSPs; global mode honors `config({jitless:true})`, while an explicit `z.compile()` call is treated as deliberate opt-in.

Generated code receives user callbacks as hoisted constants rather than interpolating their source, but those callbacks can throw or return promises and force the compiler to weaken its definitive-rejection guarantee or refuse compilation.
On invalid compiled inputs, refinements and transforms may execute twice—once in the fast path and once in interpreter fallback—so user callbacks should not rely on exactly-once side effects.

`z.jwt()` is a structural validator only: it splits three segments, decodes and parses the header, checks `typ` and `alg`, but performs no signature, issuer, audience, expiration, or claims verification.

Prototype-pollution defenses are load-bearing: object parsing strips undeclared `__proto__`, compiled records recheck transformed keys, and `assignProp` uses `Object.defineProperty` so hostile property names become own data properties.

Recursive object graphs are supported only through the memoized runtime path; cycles through transforms throw `$ZodCyclicError`, and AOT compilation refuses recursive schema subtrees because generated functions do not receive the parse context.

`fromJSONSchema` rejects external references and normalizes input with a JSON round-trip; this bounds traversal to JSON data but also means cyclic JavaScript objects, getters, proxies, class identity, and non-JSON values cannot be preserved.
The docs build sends a server-side `GITHUB_TOKEN` to GitHub GraphQL to obtain ecosystem star counts, retries failures, and intentionally fails production builds if the integration cannot supply data.
Inkeep search and chat execute in client components using `NEXT_PUBLIC_INKEEP_KEY`; the variable is intentionally browser-visible and must not be treated as a private server credential.
The Pullfrog workflow combines repository and issue write permissions with a broad set of model-provider secrets, making the third-party agent action a high-blast-radius CI trust boundary.

Publishing has write access to repository contents and OIDC, but is constrained to a manually dispatched npm environment with required approval, full prepublish checks, package availability polling, and provenance-enabled publishing.

Shared semantic changes have unusually high blast radius because interpreted containers, optionality rules, object JIT, AOT code generation, JSON Schema processors, classic, and mini must agree on key presence, output construction, and failure behavior.

extension_points.summary: Zod is extensible primarily through schema constructors, structural internals, checks, registries, callbacks, and JSON Schema processors rather than a separately loaded plugin system. Classic and mini are examples of alternate facades over the same core factory and trait machinery. Public extension hooks coexist with internal hooks such as the global construction post-processor, so consumers should distinguish supported APIs from implementation seams. The documentation site has an independent content-extension model through Fumadocs collections and MDX component mappings.

claims.claim: `core.$constructor(name, initializer, proto, params)` is the foundational schema-type extension point: it composes traits, installs prototype members, handles subclasses, runs deferred initialization, and defines trait-based `instanceof` behavior.
Core factory helpers accept a schema class parameter, allowing classic and mini constructors to share identical definition creation without importing either facade into core.

New schema behavior is represented by `$ZodTypeDef.type`, a constructor that supplies `_zod.parse`, and structural fields such as `values`, `pattern`, `propValues`, `optin`, and `optout` consumed by shared algorithms.

Checks are an extension seam: schema definitions carry a check array, each check may run attachment hooks, and classic `check`, `with`, `refine`, `superRefine`, and `overwrite` clone the schema with additional checks.

Typed metadata registries can be created with `registry()`, attach metadata through `schema.register`, inherit metadata through parent clones, and index schemas by metadata `id` for multi-schema JSON Schema output.

JSON Schema generation is extensible through a processor table keyed by schema type, per-schema `_zod.processJSONSchema` or `_zod.toJSONSchema` overrides, a global `override` callback, and an `unrepresentable` handler.

`withParser` is an explicit bridge for build-time or native compilers: a caller may install a synchronous parser returning either a fresh output or the shared `INVALID` sentinel while retaining interpreter fallback.
`globalConfig.postProcessor` is an internal construction hook used by `zod/compile`; `customError`, `localeError`, `jitless`, and `memoizer` are the supported global behavior knobs.
User callbacks extend runtime behavior through custom predicates, refinements, transforms, preprocessors, catches, codecs, lazy getters, and function-schema implementations.
Standard Schema properties provide an ecosystem integration point that does not require consumers to depend on concrete Zod classes.
Documentation is extended by adding MDX to the docs or blog collection and, when needed, mapping React components into the catch-all docs and blog renderers.

agent_handoff.summary: Future agents should treat this as a performance-sensitive library with several mutually dependent execution modes, not as a conventional web application. The safest workflow is to inspect the relevant facade, core implementation, and focused tests before making the smallest possible change. Runtime correctness alone is insufficient for changes under `packages/zod/src`; memory and bundle impact are first-class acceptance criteria. Release operations, version changes, GitHub ticket workflows, and new files all have explicit repository-specific constraints.

claims.claim: Read `AGENTS.md`, the relevant public facade, the corresponding core schema/check implementation, and the focused test file before editing; `CLAUDE.md` is only a symlink to the same instructions.
Use Nub exclusively: install with `nub install --frozen-lockfile`, run repository TypeScript with `nub`, scripts with `nub run`, and third-party tools with `nub exec --node`.

Start verification with the smallest relevant Vitest file or test name, then run broader tests; every bug fix or feature must include focused TypeScript test coverage for success, failure, and meaningful edges.
For compiler changes, run the direct compiler and differential suites plus `nub run test:compile`; compile mode is already part of the full root test command.
Any non-trivial source change must report runtime, retained-memory, and bundle-size measurements together; core changes affect every distribution, and mini requires a separate bundle-size result.

When changing constructor or property-placement machinery, preserve descriptors and instance shapes, then run the memory surface and dictionary-mode checks because accessor placement can cause large V8 regressions.
Do not add schema-type-specific branching to shared parse paths; expose capabilities structurally through internals such as `optin`, `optout`, `values`, `pattern`, or `propValues`.

Do not widen format validators solely because a specification permits more inputs; repository policy prioritizes observed producer/consumer compatibility, JSON Schema consistency, hot-path cost, and narrow defaults.
Keep comments short, avoid consecutive prose `//` lines, add no debug logging, and run `nub run check:comments` alongside format and lint checks.
Do not bump package versions or dispatch the release workflow without explicit maintainer direction; release publication is manual and protected by an npm environment approval.
For docs changes, remember that production ecosystem builds require `GITHUB_TOKEN`, content lives under `packages/docs/content`, and the build is a Next/Turbopack invocation from the docs workspace.
Run built-package resolution and integration checks after `nub run build`; source-condition tests cannot prove CommonJS, ESM, declaration, or downstream framework compatibility.

For GitHub issues or PRs, use the repository triage workflow and `gh`; contributor PR modifications belong in a worktree, and new remote branches must be pushed with an explicit refspec to avoid updating `main`.
